description: A herd of three elephants raided paddy and maize fields in the buffer zone near Minneriya National Park during the night of March 15, 2023. One farmer sustained minor injuries while attempting to drive away the elephants using firecrackers. Approximately 2.5 acres of standing paddy were damaged with estimated losses of LKR 45,000. The elephants entered through a gap in the temporary electric fence that had been disabled during routine maintenance. This was the third incident recorded at this specific location in 2023.

A 52-year-old farmer was killed by a solitary bull elephant in the Padaviya area of Anuradhapura district on June 22, 2023. The victim was returning home along a forest path at dusk when he encountered the elephant. The animal charged without warning, fatally trampling the man. This is the sixth human fatality recorded in Anuradhapura district in 2023. The elephant, identified as a large tusker known to frequent the area near Wilpattu National Park boundary, showed no provocation prior to the attack.

A herd of seven elephants, including two juveniles, raided agricultural fields bordering Lahugala Kitulana National Park in Ampara district on the night of August 10, 2023. The herd caused significant damage to paddy, sugarcane, and banana plantations across 6.8 acres owned by four farming families. Total estimated crop damage was LKR 124,000. Farmers reported that the elephants followed a well-established corridor from the national park into the farming areas. No casualties occurred as residents were alerted by a community watch tower.

Two elephants from the Somawathiya sanctuary broke into a rural homestead in Trincomalee district on September 3, 2023, causing LKR 215,000 worth of structural damage. The elephants demolished a storage shed containing rice, destroyed a water storage tank, and damaged the rear wall of the main residence. The family escaped unharmed by sheltering in the kitchen. DWC officers who responded found that the elephants had navigated around a chili pepper barrier that farmers had installed along their boundary.

A solitary male elephant injured two villagers in Ibbagamuwa, Kurunegala district on November 18, 2023. The animal was attracted to a coconut grove and charged a group of three people attempting to drive it away. Two sustained injuries — one with a fractured arm and one with lacerations — and were treated at Kurunegala General Hospital. The elephant also damaged 1.2 acres of coconut palms valued at LKR 32,000. Kurunegala is not traditionally classified as a high-HEC zone, and residents lacked access to deterrent equipment.

Five elephants raided paddy fields near Giritale tank in Polonnaruwa district on January 12, 2022. The raid lasted approximately six hours beginning at 10 PM. Farmers used drums, firecrackers, and torches to repel the herd but the elephants returned multiple times throughout the night. Total paddy losses amounted to 4.1 acres valued at LKR 73,000 across three farming families. The elephants were part of a larger aggregation that gathers near Minneriya during the dry season when water sources within the park diminish.

A night-time road collision near Tissamaharama, Hambantota district on April 27, 2022 resulted in one human fatality, three injuries, and the death of an adult female elephant. A passenger bus travelling from Kataragama struck an elephant that had wandered onto the A2 highway near the Yala National Park boundary. The bus driver died at the scene, and three passengers were hospitalised with serious injuries. The elephant, estimated to be 30 years old, died from injuries sustained in the impact. This stretch of the A2 highway is a known elephant crossing corridor and has recorded six road accidents in the past five years.

A 38-year-old rubber tapper was killed by an elephant in a rubber plantation near Bibile, Monaragala district on July 14, 2022. The victim entered the plantation at dawn, a common time for elephant activity in this region. The elephant charged from within dense vegetation without warning, killing the man instantly. Monaragala district recorded four human fatalities from elephant encounters in 2022, making it one of the most affected districts in the Uva Province. Gal Oya National Park elephants frequently move through rubber and paddy plantation corridors in this area.

A large herd of twelve elephants, including four females with calves, raided agricultural fields across three villages in Horowpathana, Anuradhapura district on October 30, 2022. The herd moved through the area for two consecutive nights, damaging paddy, sesame, and cowpea crops across 11.3 acres. Total losses for eleven farming families were estimated at LKR 186,000. This was the largest herd size documented in a Horowpathana raid event in 2022. The herd had been moving southward from the Wilpattu National Park boundary following heavy rainfall that flooded their usual feeding areas within the park.

A woman was seriously injured when a lone elephant surprised her while she was harvesting corn in a smallholder farm in Rattota, Matale district on February 8, 2021. The animal had descended from the Knuckles Conservation Forest adjacent to the cultivation area. The victim sustained a fractured pelvis and internal injuries and required three months of hospitalisation. The elephant had been seen near the same farm on two previous occasions in the preceding fortnight. The farm lacked any physical or electrical barrier, and no early warning system was in place.

A sub-adult male elephant was found dead near Maha Oya, Ampara district on May 19, 2021. A DWC post-mortem examination confirmed death by poisoning, with hakkapatas (crude explosive devices concealed in food) fragments found in the stomach contents. The elephant had reportedly been raiding crops in the area for three weeks prior to its death. This represented an illegal retaliatory killing; DWC investigators launched inquiries into the incident. Hakkapatas use remains a critical conservation concern in eastern Sri Lanka, with six confirmed elephant deaths by this method recorded in Ampara district between 2019 and 2023.

Four elephants raided paddy fields and jak fruit trees in Embilipitiya, Ratnapura district on August 22, 2021. The herd, which originated from Udawalawa National Park, had been tracked moving northward over five days before reaching the cultivation area. Three acres of paddy and 0.2 acres of jak fruit trees were damaged, valued at LKR 57,000. An electric fence on the park boundary had a gap of approximately 80 metres where posts had been removed by local residents to allow cattle movement. Udawalawa elephants using this corridor have been a recurring issue since 2018.

A 61-year-old man was killed by an elephant while walking to his paddy field at dawn in Medirigiriya, Polonnaruwa district on December 4, 2021. The elephant, a large solitary male, had been sighted in the area for several days prior. The victim had no means of communication or warning device. Medirigiriya is located within a high-frequency elephant movement zone linking Minneriya and Kaudulla national parks. This fatality was the ninth recorded in Polonnaruwa district during 2021, the highest annual count for the district in a decade.

Six elephants from Bundala National Park raided paddy and groundnut fields in the buffer zone village of Embilipitiya on March 1, 2020. The elephants exploited a dry season low water level to cross the Kirindi Oya river and access cultivation areas. Five acres of paddy and 0.5 acres of groundnut crops belonging to eight families were destroyed with total losses of LKR 98,000. This was the eleventh crop raid documented from Bundala-adjacent villages in the 2019-2020 dry season period, an 80% increase compared to the same period in 2018-2019.

A young female elephant approximately 15 years old was found dead near Medawachchiya in Anuradhapura district on July 18, 2020. Post-mortem analysis revealed electrocution as the cause of death from an illegal electrical trap set around a paddy field. Illegal electrical traps — locally called 'current fences' — are a major threat to elephant survival in north-central Sri Lanka. Farmers install these by illegally tapping power lines and running bare electric wire around their fields at a height that intercepts elephants. DWC recorded eleven elephant deaths by electrocution in Anuradhapura district between 2019 and 2022.

Two elephants moved out of Maduru Oya National Park boundary and raided paddy and corn fields in Mahiyangana, Badulla district on October 11, 2020. One farmer suffered a sprained shoulder when struck by the elephant's trunk while attempting to chase the animals with a lighted torch. Crop losses totaled 1.9 acres valued at LKR 34,500. Mahiyangana lies on the eastern edge of the Uva Province where growing agricultural encroachment has reduced the effective buffer between the national park and farming villages, making this a recurring conflict zone.

Two men from the same farming family were killed by an elephant near the Arugam Bay hinterland in Ampara district on April 16, 2019. The two men — a father and son — were tending a chena plot at dusk when they encountered a lone bull elephant. Both were killed at the scene. This double fatality drew significant attention from wildlife authorities and media. Post-incident investigation revealed the elephant had a history of aggressive behaviour documented at Lahugala park. DWC initiated a GPS collaring programme for this individual to monitor movement. This was one of the highest-profile HEC fatality events recorded in eastern Sri Lanka in recent years.

A herd of approximately twenty elephants — part of the dry-zone elephant aggregation known as the Kaudulla Gathering — raided paddy fields bordering Kaudulla National Park in Polonnaruwa district in September 2019. The raid caused one of the largest single-event crop losses documented in Polonnaruwa during 2019, with 18.6 acres of standing paddy destroyed across eleven farming households. Total losses reached LKR 321,000. September coincides with the peak dry-season gathering at Kaudulla, when water availability within the park is highest and elephant numbers are greatest. Agricultural encroachment into the buffer zone has steadily increased the frequency of boundary violations.

Three elephants damaged five residential structures in the Kantale area of Trincomalee district on November 27, 2019. The elephants moved through the outskirts of the town during the early morning hours. Two houses had their walls partially demolished and stored food was consumed. Three other structures sustained minor damage. The total estimated property damage was LKR 175,000. Kantale has seen increasing elephant intrusions since 2017 linked to the depletion of natural food sources in adjacent forest patches. Residents reported no effective deterrent system in the village.

A 45-year-old farmer was killed by an elephant near Kebithigollewa village in Anuradhapura district on January 30, 2024. The man had gone to irrigate his paddy field early in the morning when the incident occurred. Witnesses reported the elephant charged from a forested area along the field boundary. Kebithigollewa has one of the highest per-capita rates of human-elephant conflict fatalities in Sri Lanka; the community has recorded over 20 human deaths from elephant attacks since 2010. Residents have repeatedly petitioned for improved early warning systems and electric fence maintenance in the area.

Eight elephants raided crops across multiple farms in Buttala, Monaragala district on March 14, 2024. The raid extended over two consecutive nights, with paddy, corn, and cowpea across 7.4 acres damaged, costing farmers approximately LKR 132,000. Buttala sits at the northern boundary of Yala National Park's Block V and has been designated a conflict hotspot by the DWC since 2020. Local farmers report that beehive fences installed by an NGO project in 2022 have reduced incidents along one boundary but the herd circumvented them through an unfenced creek corridor.

A young bull elephant approximately 20 years old was found dead near Hingurakgoda in Polonnaruwa district on May 22, 2024. Veterinary post-mortem examination identified gun-shot wounds as the cause of death. Three pellets from a shotgun were recovered from the body cavity. DWC investigators believe the elephant was killed by farmers protecting their crops, as the site of discovery was adjacent to extensive paddy cultivation. Retaliatory killings using firearms remain an under-reported phenomenon in Sri Lanka. DWC formally requested police investigation, emphasising that Sri Lankan elephants are fully protected under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance.

Three people were injured when an elephant entered Nikaweratiya town in Kurunegala district on July 9, 2024. The elephant, a young male, entered from a forest patch at the town boundary and moved through a market area before being guided back by DWC officers. Three bystanders sustained injuries while attempting to flee the area. One paddy field at the town edge was also damaged. The incident highlighted the expansion of HEC into peri-urban areas of Kurunegala district, which has experienced a 40% increase in elephant-related incidents over the past three years as forest corridors connecting isolated elephant populations have been fragmented by development.

Four elephants raided paddy and vegetable plots in Uhana, Ampara district on September 17, 2024. The herd caused losses of LKR 51,000 across 2.8 acres. This location had previously been protected by a solar-powered electric fence installed under a government-NGO partnership in 2021, but the fence had fallen into disrepair due to lack of maintenance funding. Uhana farmers have raised the issue of fence maintenance sustainability as a systemic problem, noting that initial installation is funded but long-term maintenance responsibility remains unclear between the DWC, local authorities, and farming communities.
